data.caption: drjamescummings.com
data.copy:
In 2003, a senior Pfizer researcher named Dr. Donald Mitchell walked away from a $340,000 salary and 19 years with the company.

In his exit interview, he said something that should terrify every man taking ED pills: "We know what actually restores erectile function. We're just not allowed to sell it because you can't patent a natural solution.”

Today, Donald is 71 years old.

He hasn't taken Viagra in 18 years.

And according to his wife Catherine (who agreed to be interviewed), they're still having sex 2-3 times per day. Yes… per day.

"Most of our friends stopped having sex in their 60s," Catherine said. "Their husbands are on pills that barely work. Donald does something different."

What Donald discovered during his time at Pfizer changed everything he thought he knew about erectile dysfunction. And it has nothing to do with the blue pill.

The Pfizer Files: What They Found (And Buried)

During Donald's tenure in Pfizer's vascular research division, the team was tasked with understanding why Viagra worked for some men but failed for others.

The drug worked by forcing blood vessels to dilate temporarily. But in clinical trials, 30-40% of men saw zero improvement.

The drug forced their vessels open, but blood still wouldn't flow properly.

Donald's team discovered why: These men had depleted levels of a molecule called nitric oxide.

Nitric oxide is the molecule that signals your blood vessels to relax, open up, and fill with blood naturally. After age 40, your body produces roughly 10% less every year. By 55, you've lost nearly half of what you had at 30. By 65, you're running on fumes.

Without nitric oxide, your blood vessels stay constricted. Blood can't flow freely. Not to your penis. Not to your brain. Not anywhere.

Viagra tries to force the plumbing open. But if you are experiencing Nitric Oxide Collapse, the signal never gets sent. It's like trying to open a door by pushing harder when the lock is broken. That’s why it stops working over time an…

My husband and I slept at his ex wife's house during a flood. We did it in her bed.

And it saved our marriage.

Last September, Bill and I were driving back from his mother's 80th birthday when the rain started. Not normal rain. The kind where you can't see the car in front of you and the highway turns into a river in twenty minutes.

We pulled over twice. It got worse. By 9pm, the roads near our house were closed. Water over the bridges. No way home until morning at the earliest.

Bill looked at his phone. Then at me.

'Sharon lives ten minutes from here.'

Sharon. His ex wife. Married to her for six years before me. Divorced twenty years ago. They're civil. Christmas cards. Happy birthdays to the kids. She came to his mother's 70th birthday. Nice enough.

But I'd never been inside her house.

'Bill, we are not staying at your ex wife's house.'

'Donna, the roads are closed. We're not sleeping in the car.'

He called her. She said of course. Come over. Guest room is all yours.

I sat in the passenger seat with my arms crossed like a teenager.

'One night,' I said.
'One night,' he said.

We pulled into her driveway at 9:30. I checked my reflection in the visor mirror. No makeup. Hair pulled back. Wearing the oversized fleece and leggings I'd thrown on for a three-hour car ride to his mother's house.

Sharon opened the door in a silk robe. Hair down. Smelled like vanilla.

Of course she did.

She hugged Bill. The kind of hug where her hand touched the back of his neck for just a second longer than it needed to.

Then she hugged me. 'Donna, I'm so glad you're both safe. Come in, come in.'

Her house was warm. Not just the temperature. Everything. Candles on the entryway table. Soft lighting. Music playing quietly from somewhere. A throw blanket draped over a leather chair that looked like someone had just been curled up in it reading.

The house smelled like a woman who was expecting company even when she wasn't.

My babysitter canceled the same day I had a job interview at one of the biggest companies in the city.

So I brought my daughter, told her to stay put in the lobby, and promised I’d be quick.

But the interview went horribly, I stumbled over my words, spilled coffee over my resume, and the manager barely looked up when she said, “We’ll let you know.”

When I came back out, my daughter was gone.

I ran through the lobby, calling her name, until I heard laughter coming from the corner office at the end of the hall.

I swung the door open and there she was, sitting cross-legged on the floor, showing her crayon drawings to the billionaire CEO.

He looked up, and his smile flickered into something softer the moment our eyes met.

Then turned back to my daughter’s drawing and said,

“I like her style. What do you say we bring you both on board?”

data.caption: Read this if your puppy WON'T potty train 👆
data.copy:
Six months ago, I thought potty training my golden retriever puppy was just going to take patience.

Now I was scrubbing urine out of my bedroom carpet at 6 AM for the third time that week.

Luna was six months old. Half a year of accidents. Half a year of coming home to mystery puddles. Half a year of that smell that never quite left no matter how much enzyme cleaner I used.

You know what's worse than the accidents themselves?

It's the unpredictability.

March, when I first brought her home, it was maybe once a day. I could handle that. She was eight weeks old. Puppies have accidents. Everyone said it would get better.

April. Twice a day. Sometimes three times. But she was still small, so the puddles were manageable. I bought more paper towels. More cleaner. Told myself it was temporary.

May. I stopped counting. The accidents weren't decreasing. They were just happening. Randomly. No pattern I could identify. I'd take her outside, she'd do nothing, we'd come back in, and ten minutes later there'd be a puddle by the couch.

June. The month I realized this wasn't getting better on its own.

I'd tried everything the internet suggested. Crate training. Taking her out every hour. Treating her when she went outside. Watching her like a hawk for "signs." (What signs? She gave no signs.) Restricting water. Not restricting water. Different schedules.

Nothing worked.

And the worst part? Luna was the sweetest dog I'd ever had. She was cuddly and playful and so eager to please. Like that time she accidentally bit my arm while chewing her antler and immediately crawled into my lap to apologize with face licks. She wasn't being bad. She just... didn't understand where she was supposed to go when we were inside.

But I was drowning.

My apartment smelled. I knew it did. I'd become nose-blind to it, but I saw how my sister hesitated at the door when she visited. How my coworker made an excuse when I offered to carpool.

I couldn't have people over anymore.

data.caption: Korea solved melasma 10 years ago. We didn't listen.
data.copy:
I flew to Seoul to interview one of Korea's top dermatologists about melasma.
What she told me made me angry at the entire Western skincare industry.
I'm a beauty editor. I've written about skincare for 9 years. I've interviewed dermatologists in New York, Los Angeles, London, and Paris. I've tested hundreds of products. I've sat through press events where brands present "revolutionary breakthroughs" that are really just Vitamin C in a new bottle.
I thought I understood melasma. I'd written three articles about it. The narrative was always the same. Melasma is chronic, triggered by hormones and sun, managed with hydroquinone and sunscreen, and sometimes treated with careful laser work. No cure. Just management.
Then last September, a Korean skincare brand sent me a product to review. A cream with Tranexamic Acid at 70,000 ppm. I'd heard of Tranexamic Acid in passing. It was on my "ingredients to watch" list. But I didn't know much about it.
I did what I always do. I started reading the research.
What I found shocked me.
There are over 22 published randomized controlled trials on Tranexamic Acid for melasma. Twenty-two. This isn't fringe science. This isn't a TikTok trend. This is a deeply studied molecule with a decade of clinical evidence.
And Korean dermatologists have been using it as a first-line treatment for melasma since the early 2010s.
While we were prescribing hydroquinone with a 3-month limit and watching patients rebound, Korean clinics were giving patients Tranexamic Acid, topically and orally, and seeing sustained improvement without rebound.
I had to see it for myself.
I booked a flight to Seoul. I contacted Dr. Yoon, a board-certified dermatologist who runs one of Seoul's busiest pigmentation clinics. She agreed to an interview.
Her clinic was in Gangnam. Clean, minimal, packed with patients. The waiting room was full of women between 25 and 55. Most of them were there for melasma.

data.caption: My mother had hip surgery at 61. She was never the same.
data.copy:
My mother had her hip replaced when she was sixty-one. She was never the same after. I swore I would not end up like her.

My mother was a nurse for thirty-four years. Worked the night shift at a hospital in Hamilton. She had been on her feet her whole adult life, transferring patients, lifting, walking the same fluorescent corridors twelve hours at a stretch. She was the strongest woman I knew.

She had osteoarthritis in her left hip. For a long time, she managed.

Then the pain got worse. Her doctor sent her to an orthopaedic surgeon. The surgeon told her the cartilage was worn, the joint was bone-on-bone, and she needed a replacement. She went on the surgical list and had the operation in the spring of her sixty-first year.

The surgery itself went fine. That is what the surgeon kept saying afterwards. The surgery went fine. The X-rays looked perfect. The new hardware was seated exactly where it was supposed to be.

But she was not fine.

The hip on that side never bent the way the other one did. She walked with a small hitch nobody could explain. The thigh muscle around the new joint never came back — six months of physiotherapy and it stayed soft and weak. She got a deep ache where the incision had been that would flare in cold weather and never fully leave her alone again.

She started favouring the other hip. Within four years that hip needed replacing too. She had the second surgery at sixty-five.

By the time she was seventy, she was using a cane in the house. By seventy-three, a walker.

She told me once, near the end, that the worst thing about the surgeries was not the pain afterwards. The worst thing was that the woman who got off the operating table was never quite the woman who got on it. She said it the way you would describe a relative who had been replaced by an imposter. Something is missing. I cannot tell you what it is. But I know it.

She died at seventy-six.

data.caption: My trade took a toll on me
data.copy:
I was two weeks away from taking a $60K pay cut to get off the tools.

Forty-five years old. Been a chippy since I was eighteen. Twenty-seven years doing something I actually love.

And I was about to walk away from it because my body couldn't handle it anymore.

Started about twelve months ago with my feet. Standing on concrete all day, they'd ache by knock-off. Nothing major at first. Just sore. Figured it was a long week, she'll be right.

But it didn't get right. It got worse.

By six months in, my feet were killing me. Proper pain. Every step felt like walking on rocks. Sharp, jabbing pain that shot up from my heels. By the end of a shift it felt like someone had taken a hammer to the bottom of my feet. I'd be limping to my ute trying not to let anyone see, every step sending this burning sensation straight up my legs.

Then my knees started aching. Constant. Couldn't kneel without wincing. My lower back started seizing up every afternoon.

My seven-year-old daughter started mimicking the way I walk when I get home. Hunched over, shuffling. "Dad you walk like a penguin!" she'd say, waddling around the kitchen. She thought it was hilarious. I laughed with her but it destroyed me inside.

Then two months ago I spent a full day screwing in ceiling tiles and my shoulder flared up bad. Burning pain. Couldn't lift properly. Two weeks later it was still rooted.
Everything hurt. Feet. Knees. Back. Shoulder.

Whole body falling apart and I'm only forty-five.

Makes you feel weak when you can't hold up to the work anymore. Especially when you're alongside blokes barely younger than you who seem fine. I used to think I got paid to work out. Twenty years ago I'd finish a hard day and feel strong. Now I finish a shift and everything's screaming.

Sucks getting older.

I'd heard the stories. Tough blokes who had to leave the tools in their late forties because their bodies couldn't handle it. Figured maybe that's just what happens. You get your time and then it's done.

website.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: SH, TP, BU, LS, CC, SL, TA, GG, FU, CS, LP, FO, SI, GP, XS, YC, HY, DI, MS, SB, PP, WC, TT, TW, PI, GO, SC, FB, MG, WP, SQ, PS, GM, KV, CO, HJ, WX, AR, BC, MC. SH=Shopify, WC=WooCommerce, CS=Clickfunnels. See allowed_technologies in response.

languages.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

excludeLanguages.allowed_values: Comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

apps.description: Shopify apps detected on the store.
apps.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated app names/ids from dashboard Apps filter. See allowed_apps in response.

excludeApps.description: Exclude stores using these Shopify apps.
excludeApps.allowed_values: Comma-separated app names/ids. See allowed_apps in response.

themes.description: Shopify theme name on the store (exact match).
themes.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated exact theme names from dashboard Themes filter (discover via GET /api/themes).

scaling.allowed_values: rising, stable, declining, nodownscaling, upscaling, downscaling.

mediafilter.allowed_values: videos, images, carousel, dco. Omit/All = all formats.

pagetypefilter.allowed_values: products, collections, funnels, nofunnels. Empty/All = all types.

adscorefilter.description: WinningHunter ad score tier (Established / Has Potential / Unestablished).
adscorefilter.allowed_values: winning (Established), scaling (Has Potential), testing (Unestablished). Requires matching account tier.

lowimpressions.description: Hide ads with very low impressions.
lowimpressions.allowed_values: hide (exclude low-impression rows). Omit = show all.

rankgrowthfilter.description: Within-brand ad rank momentum vs historic rank_history.
rankgrowthfilter.allowed_values: Comma-separated subset of: rising, stable, declining.

minadrank.description: Minimum within-brand ad rank (lower rank number = stronger ad for that brand, e.g. #1).

min.description: Minimum duplicate/active-seen ad count on the page.

minactiveads.description: Minimum active Meta ads on the advertiser Facebook page (total_active_ads_on_page).
minactiveads.notes: find_winning_products auto-applies minactiveads=50 for US when not set (see forced block).

minactiveadsgrowth.description: Minimum page active-ads percent growth over activeadsgrowthperiod.
minactiveadsgrowth.allowed_values: Human percent (25 = 25%); negatives allowed for decline.

activeadsgrowthperiod.description: Lookback window for active-ads growth filter.
activeadsgrowthperiod.allowed_values: 1w, 1m, 3m. Default 1m when min/max growth set. 1w=1 week, 1m=1 month, 3m=3 months.
activeadsgrowthperiod.notes: 14d/2m exist on the dashboard but are omitted from MCP — sparse wlads baselines return empty result sets.

minpagelikes.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. Ads missing the field excluded when min set.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.
